{"id": "94:3/q07", "question": "What was the burden that weighed on the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Which experience is understood as the oppressive load, and whether it denotes actual sin, protected innocence, the mission, or distress about the Prophet and his people.", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q07/p1", "position": "His own sins or earlier lapses, removed by forgiveness.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī, Qatāda, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk report sins; al-Ṭabarī connects forgiveness with days of ignorance. Ibn Zayd places them before prophethood; al-Wāḥidī, Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī and Asad specify pre-mission acts or mistakes. Some qualify them as minor sins, errors, or inadvertence; al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Mufaḍḍal specifies the latter. Elmalılı cites 6:31 and 48:2 for this reading, but rejects its fit with prophetic minor lapses."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p2", "position": "The responsibilities of prophethood, revelation, warning, and conveying the message.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says the message weighed until delivery; al-Kisāʾī, Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā and Abū ʿUbayda describe duties, preservation and rights made manageable. Biqāʿī stresses warning people who resented criticism of their faith and ancestors; 5:67 promises protection. Qutb says God opened hearts and sent clarifying revelation. Elmalılı adds fear of failure, 35:28, Gabriel's awe in 53:5–6, hostility, and eventual habituation. Qāshānī gives an inward reading: return from exclusive witnessing to prophetic commands nearly broke the heart's veil, until abiding empowered unity amid multiplicity."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p3", "position": "His bewilderment and lack of a clear path before revelation.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Elmalılı describe a conscience troubled by God's unrepayable gifts without knowledge of how to serve Him; service through prophethood eased the shame. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī mention perplexity, including the mission's reception. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ agrees with ʿAbduh, linking confusion to 93:7. Iṣlāḥī adds unanswered truth-seeking and delayed revelation."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p4", "position": "Distress over his people's error, idolatry, and refusal of guidance.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 16:123: Abraham's religion was being changed before Muhammad had power to intervene. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī describe inability to guide the resistant; al-Ālūsī names Ḥamza and ʿUmar's conversion as relief. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ corrects al-Ḍaḥḥāk's 'shirk' to the people's shirk; ʿAbduh calls the concern psychologically crushing. Iṣlāḥī cites 20:1–3 about preaching not intended to distress; Kur'an Yolu favors relief through revelation and social support."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p5", "position": "Persecution, insults, and threats directed at him by his people.", "reasons": "Rāzī says God strengthened him to bear even a bloodied face, when he prayed for their guidance. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī mention persistent abuse. Biqāʿī recounts fears of his head being split, relatives restraining his preaching, and divine support under 5:67. Elmalılı cites 5:67 and 93:4–5 for protection or hope."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p6", "position": "The sins of his community, borne through concern for them.", "reasons": "Rāzī says reassurance came through 8:33 and promised intercession. Al-Qurṭubī says their sins occupied his heart. Al-Ālūsī reports removal as withholding immediate punishment while the Prophet remained or they sought forgiveness, but calls the interpretation remote."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p7", "position": "He was protected from sin and pre-revelation impurity, so no actual sin burden existed.", "reasons": "Al-Muḥāsibī says the burden would have weighed had God not pardoned him. Rāzī illustrates protection by the wedding story: God put him to sleep before he could join music. Al-Qurṭubī says he was pure for forty years; Abū Ḥayyān calls the apparent removal a hyperbolic figure for purification. Al-Rāghib says he was exempted from pre-Islamic customs; al-Ālūsī reports Abū Ḥayyān's view."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p8", "position": "His ignorance of revealed rulings before God taught them.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī, and later survey notes distinguish this absence of legal knowledge from uncertainty about the mission; revelation removed it."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p9", "position": "The initial terror and weight of Gabriel's appearance or reception of revelation.", "reasons": "Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī describe trembling and fear at the first encounter, even a near leap from a mountain; Gabriel's appearance relieved fear that his reason had changed. Elmalılı invokes the mighty angel in 53:5–6, then gradual adaptation."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p10", "position": "Grief after the deaths of Abū Ṭālib and Khadīja.", "reasons": "Rāzī and al-Ālūsī condition this reading on the sūra's revelation after their deaths; ascension, angels' greeting, raised renown, and beholding the Lord are described as consolation."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p11", "position": "Blessings that required gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī lists gifts as a possible weight until the Prophet gave thanks. Elmalılı notes the shame of enjoying gifts without a way to serve the giver."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p12", "position": "The pause in revelation and the resulting loneliness and mockery.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says interruption increased worldly and otherworldly anxiety; resumed revelation and al-Ḍuḥā brought relief."}, {"id": "94:3/q07/p13", "position": "Practical insecurity and livelihood that distracted from reform.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says God removed part of the burden through guidance to truth and provision for livelihood, citing 93:7–8."}]}
{"id": "94:3/q08", "question": "Why could forgiven sins still weigh so heavily?", "turns_on": "Whether the continuing weight comes from remorse, uncertain completion of repentance, or the cost in reward.", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q08/p1", "position": "The Prophet and the righteous deeply regret and grieve even over forgiven lapses.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, al-Muḥāsibī and al-Qurṭubī stress continuing sorrow. Rāzī attributes intense remorse to those who allow minor prophetic sins. Elmalılı reports the alternative that exceptional sensitivity makes even a small lapse heavy."}, {"id": "94:3/q08/p2", "position": "The righteous fear they have not yet fulfilled every duty of complete repentance.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās offers this as another explanation for the burden's persistence."}, {"id": "94:3/q08/p3", "position": "Even a minor sin could forfeit a great reward.", "reasons": "Rāzī records this separate defense of calling the lapse weighty."}]}
{"id": "94:3/q09", "question": "Does the burden wording establish a view on prophetic impeccability?", "turns_on": "Whether the image presupposes committed sin or is a rhetorical way to describe protection.", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q09/p1", "position": "It may describe actual minor sin and forgiveness, which is a divine favor.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports the permissive view but objects to the Qāḍī's claim that forgiveness of minor sins is obligatory for God: a mandatory pardon could not be praised as a favor. {"id": "94:3/q10", "question": "How was the burden lifted or made bearable?", "turns_on": "The answer follows which burden is identified.", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q10/p1", "position": "God forgave prior sins or prevented a burden of sin.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd and others identify forgiveness; al-Muḥāsibī and Abū Ḥayyān frame relief as pardon or prior protection. Elmalılı describes habituation, insight, spiritual strength and al-Ḍuḥā; al-Ālūsī notes practice. Biqāʿī invokes signs, miracles and 5:67; his account of Gabriel cleansing the black clot and filling the heart with knowledge, faith and wisdom explains capacity. Qāshānī's inward account names empowerment in abiding."}, {"id": "94:3/q10/p3", "position": "God taught religious law and gave direction for service.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says revealed knowledge ended its absence. Rāzī and Elmalılı say revelation and duty answered the Prophet's question of how to repay blessings and follow Abraham, citing 16:123."}, {"id": "94:3/q10/p4", "position": "God guided some of his people and supported the establishment of monotheism and virtue.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī names Ḥamza and ʿUmar's conversion. Kur'an Yolu mentions justice, honesty, mercy and cooperation; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 93:7–8 for guidance and provision."}, {"id": "94:3/q10/p5", "position": "He was consoled by ascension and the raising of his renown.", "reasons": "Rāzī and al-Ālūsī connect this conditionally to the deaths of Abū Ṭālib and Khadīja; the angels greeted him, and al-Ālūsī adds beholding his Lord."}, {"id": "94:3/q10/p6", "position": "God reassured him about the community and withheld immediate punishment.", "reasons": "Rāzī mentions later intercession and 8:33. {"id": "94:3/q13", "question": "Was al-Sharḥ a separate sūra, and when and for whom was it revealed?", "turns_on": "The transmission about its unity with sūra 93 and competing chronological reports.", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q13/p1", "position": "It follows al-Ḍuḥā closely and addresses the Prophet first, then Qurʾān followers.", "reasons": "Asad dates it almost immediately after al-Ḍuḥā and extends the address through the Prophet to true followers."}, {"id": "94:3/q13/p2", "position": "The two chapters were treated as one by some reciters.", "reasons": "Asad attributes this to Ṭāwūs and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, citing Rāzī; Study Quran says some Companions recited both in one prayer cycle without a second basmala."}, {"id": "94:3/q13/p3", "position": "Most call it Makkan after sūra 93; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it Madinan, and some assign only verses 5–6 to Madinah.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the competing place assignments."}]}
{"id": "94:3/q14", "question": "What reports or comparisons are cited to illuminate the Prophet's preparation and the sūra's favors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q14/p1", "position": "Gabriel opened and washed the Prophet's chest, then filled it with knowledge, faith and wisdom.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reports Ibn ʿAbbās's black-clot account and infers that it equipped the Prophet to bear what others could not."}, {"id": "94:3/q14/p2", "position": "A report likens reciting the sūra to visiting the distressed Prophet and relieving him.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī reports this statement attributed to the Prophet."}, {"id": "94:3/q14/p3", "position": "A report in which the Prophet asks why others got special favors is criticized.", "reasons": "The Qāḍī says prophets ask only by permission and that God's reply in the report sounds reproachful."}]}

{"id": "94:3/q16", "question": "What other recitation and linguistic examples accompany discussion of this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q16/p1", "position": "In a sākin ṭāʾ followed by tāʾ, assimilation remains incomplete to preserve emphasis.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī calls ṭāʾ the strongest emphatic letter."}, {"id": "94:3/q16/p2", "position": "A sākin ẓāʾ before tāʾ is normally clear, though Ibn Muḥayṣin assimilated it while retaining emphasis.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports the imams' agreement on clarity and Ibn Muḥayṣin's variant."}, {"id": "94:3/q16/p3", "position": "Preserve ʿayn before a voiceless letter and distinguish it from ghayn; keep ghayn clear, especially near qāf.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī warns against emphatic ʿayn and against moving ghayn in lā tuzigh qulūbanā."}, {"id": "94:3/q16/p4", "position": "The poetic expression qaḍḍihā bi-qaḍīḍihā denotes a mass rush and illustrates Arabic case analogy.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites al-Shammākh and notes some Arabs inflect qaḍḍihim like kullihim."}]}

{"id": "94:3/q18", "question": "What broader claims appear alongside this verse's discussion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:3/q18/p1", "position": "The Qurʾān's unanswered challenge demonstrates its inimitability.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī argues Quraysh's eloquent speakers and poets could have answered with a short sūra more cheaply than war but did not for twenty-three years."}]}

{"id": "94:4/q06", "question": "What follows from joining the Prophet's mention to God's?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different consequences for testimony, obedience, communal honor and the benefit of fame.", "positions": [{"id": "94:4/q06/p1", "position": "Faith and worship require acknowledgment of Muhammad as God's messenger.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata and Tustari say faith is completed by naming him; Ibn Ata says Messenger implies Lord. {"id": "94:4/q07", "question": "What did reports say God told the Prophet about his raised mention?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in setting, wording and added gifts to the Prophet or his community.", "positions": [{"id": "94:4/q07/p1", "position": "Gabriel relayed that whenever God is mentioned, Muhammad is mentioned with Him.", "reasons": "The Abu Said report is widespread. {"id": "94:6/q05", "question": "What concrete ease is promised?", "turns_on": "Whether the two occurrences designate distinct worldly events, this life and the next, a broad kind of relief, or a spiritual counterpart.", "positions": [{"id": "94:6/q05/p1", "position": "Victory and relief from the polytheists.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and al-Baghawī expect the Prophet's eventual triumph and their submission to truth, willingly or under compulsion. {"id": "94:6/q07", "question": "Why is the assurance repeated?", "turns_on": "Whether repetition itself adds a distinct promise or instead reinforces the first, and whether the sequence describes recurring cycles.", "positions": [{"id": "94:6/q07/p1", "position": "It confirms one promise and strengthens hope.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites 102:3–4, 75:34–35 and 82:17–18; al-Māwardī transmits al-Farrāʾ's repeated answers and al-Khansāʾ's poem. {"id": "94:6/q17", "question": "What is reported about this surah's revelation and its relation to Sūrah 93?", "turns_on": "Whether the two surahs were revealed and recited as separate units, and which chronology is accepted.", "positions": [{"id": "94:6/q17/p1", "position": "Most call it Meccan and place it just after Sūrah 93.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports the majority chronology; Asad says revelation followed al-Ḍuḥā almost immediately."}, {"id": "94:6/q17/p2", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls it Medinan, or some assign only verses 5–6 to Medina.", "reasons": "The Study Quran records these minority chronology reports."}, {"id": "94:6/q17/p3", "position": "Some treated Sūrahs 93 and 94 as one and recited them without a second basmala.", "reasons": "Asad names Ṭāwūs ibn Kaysān and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, citing al-Rāzī; the Study Quran similarly reports Companion practice in one prayer cycle."}]}
{"id": "94:6/q18", "question": "What inward reading is given to the hardship and ease?", "turns_on": "Whether ease is future recompense and reliance or present unveiling within spiritual trial.", "positions": [{"id": "94:6/q18/p1", "position": "Worldly restraint or confinement becomes reliance on God and Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq pairs worldly effort with Paradise; al-Jawzajānī pairs abstaining from forbidden and doubtful things with the dignity of reliance; al-Qāsim contrasts the fortunate's move from worldly prison to afterlife delight with the wretched's continuing constraint."}, {"id": "94:6/q18/p2", "position": "Hardship and ease are stages of spiritual unveiling.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī's two veils, by creation from God and by God from creation, give way to disclosure through sainthood and expansion through prophethood. {"id": "94:7/q03", "question": "What does the omitted object of 'when you finish' cover?", "turns_on": "Whether omission gives broad scope or a specific contextual completion.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q03/p1", "position": "It is deliberately omitted to cover whatever important duties the context supplies.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Prophet's known demanding mission supplies the contextual category, with multiple tasks ordered by priority; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ calls omission a Qurʾānic way to keep an already understood activity open."}, {"id": "94:7/q03/p2", "position": "It is a particular finished activity: prayer, worldly work, campaign, mission, or relief.", "reasons": "Reported specifications supply particular tasks; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ lists prayer, jihad, and worldly work, while herself preferring release from distress in 94:1–4."}]}
